claims.text: Molecular dynamics simulations can be used to study the thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles.
Advanced free-energy sampling methods such as metadynamics or replica exchange are suitable enhancements for this thermal-response study.
Smaller equiatomic FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles have lower free-energy barriers for phase transitions than larger nanoparticles.
The lower transition barriers in smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are caused by increased surface-driven atomic mobility.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are equiatomic.
The initial FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles form a solid-solution phase at room temperature.
Temperature-ramped MD over nanoparticle diameters of approximately 2–10 nm can resolve size-dependent thermal behavior.
Heating simulations from approximately 298 K to 1000 K cover a relevant range for studying structural thermal evolution in these nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles have a greater fraction of surface atoms because of their higher surface-to-volume ratio.
A greater fraction of surface atoms enhances atomic diffusion and structural rearrangement.
Atomic mobility at free surfaces reduces the free-energy barriers for structural reorganization or phase transitions.
Advanced free-energy sampling integrated with MD can capture the proposed barrier reduction.
The enhanced surface mobility of smaller nanoparticles causes phase changes to begin at lower temperatures.
As FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle size decreases, phase-transition free-energy barriers and transition temperatures decrease.
Previous standard MD simulations without enhanced free-energy sampling showed less pronounced size-dependent thermal behavior.
The predicted size dependence applies to sub-10 nm FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles between approximately 300 K and 1000 K.
Quantitative free-energy barriers and transition temperatures depend on simulation details and the selected interatomic potential.
